newsitem.title: USA: US VIEW-Farmers want tough action against Australia, Canada.
newsitem.headline: US VIEW-Farmers want tough action against Australia, Canada.

text.p: European subsidies continue to cause concern for wheat exporters but despite heavy industry lobbying, the United States will resist using the Export Enhancement Program (EEP) while stocks remain in relatively short supply, according to leading officials.

"Right now we have a situation where we are making sales for our wheat and we don't anticipate a big buildup," said Chris Goldthwait, who oversees the United States Department of Agriculture's policies on export programmes.
"However if we were in a situation where we held large and ample supplies and we saw the EU was pricing very aggressively as they have been then we might not have a choice," he said.
"But right now we don't have it on a supply basis."

After a disastrous few years the U.S. wheat industry is possibly on the rebound with production up and exporters eyeing opportunities like a recent Pakistan tender for 450,000 tonnes which Australia passed on due to lack of spare capacity.
But the mood among farm lobbyists in Washington remains grim with many urging tougher action against the EU and countries like Australia and Canada with what they see as unfair state run monopolies.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), they protest, has manipulative powers which has a greater impact on world price than use of EEP.

"They sit back and watch this market, which unlike their's, is very transparent, then they set the price accordingly," said one leading bureaucrat who asked not to be named. "They don't hold back any supply ... they just put it all out there."
Some lobbyists, like Winston Wilson, president of U.S. Wheat Associates insists the EEP be used to counter the European policies and organisations like the AWB.

At the USDA's Outlook conference in Washington recently, there was significant support for EEP and in their long-term baseline projections the USDA indicated use of the programme over the next few years would be necessary.

"Generally nobody wants to 'EEP' .... but it's necessary until others barriers to the market are eliminated," Wilson said. "Basically state trading needs to go, it's a simple as that. It's probably going to take a while but eventually Australia and Canada will catch up with the times."
Australia's 'single desk' approach to wheat export through the AWB has helped the country move into new markets and operate arguably the world's most efficent export service.
Al Conway, of wheat traders Romak, said there was much to be admired in the AWB.
"They do a great job, the sort of job a lot of U.S.producers would like to see done for them," he said.
"I suppose the big objection is the AWB is not transparent enough," he said.
Goldthwait said U.S. objections to the AWB would be strenuously pursued through the WTO.
The AWB's North American vice president, Peter Geary, agreed the push for governments to get out of agriculture meant Australia was at a crossroads.
"There's talk about disciplines being placed on state trading enterprises (STEs)," he said, noting a Geneva working group was considering the situation.
"The thing we will want to get across is the need to define differences between STEs rather than simply using this generic term and assuming they are all the same," Geary said.

Geary said the war of words was likely to continue in the run down to world trade talks in 1999 but added that most exporting nations would prefer that subsidies be gradually eliminated from the market.
Despite U.S. objections to the structure of the AWB, most industry leaders point to the policies of the EU as the major problem facing exporters.
"They are really the focus, but there are some encouraging signs," Goldthwait said.
Geary agreed but added that the U.S. had marked US$500 million for use in EEP if required.
"Our focus needs to be on all export subsidies," he said.
"We can't let our guard down," he said.
"While they are not using EEP at the moment ... these things can turn around very, very quickly."
